examples: The game was canceled because of the rain.
The plan was ruined because of his mistake.
Because I stayed up all night, I'm unbearably sleepy today.
I was late because of a traffic jam.
This medicine gave me a headache.
Vegetables are expensive, perhaps because there was so much rain.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize the "negativity" of the cause or to imply blame.
Avoid using it with positive results; when the result is good, use ～おかげで.
Usable in both spoken and written language; in formal documents it can be replaced with ～ために／～により to neutralize the nuance.
Usually combined with a specific, clear cause (N/V); rarely used with Aい/Aな.

• Expresses a cause with a negative nuance, assigning blame: "because of/due to ... (bad result)".
• The speaker usually implies reproach, complaint, or a negative feeling about the cause.
• Compared with ～ために/～ので/～から: ～せいで leans toward the emotional sense of "it's the fault of (blameworthy)".
• Often used as N のせいで and Vたせいで when the cause has already happened.
• ～せいか: "maybe it's because of... that...", expresses uncertainty about the cause.
fields.notes:
• ～せいだ is the concluding form: "It's because of...". ～せいで links cause and result.
• "気のせい" is an idiom: "just one's imagination/a misperception". Example: 気のせいかもしれない。
• Avoid ～せいで in contexts that require neutrality (reports, news), as the nuance of blame may be inappropriate.
meaning_vi: Because of... / Due to... (bad result, reproach)
Not certain, perhaps because of...
explain: States the cause that led to a bad result, with a nuance of reproach.
Expresses an uncertain conjecture: "perhaps it is because of...", a milder nuance than ～せい.
examples: 1. あの人のせいでみんなが迷惑している。
Everyone is bothered because of that person.
2. 景気が悪いせいでボーナスが減った。
Bonuses were cut because of the poor economy.
3. 試合に負けたのはミスをした私のせいだ。
We lost the game because I made a mistake.
4. 大気汚染が悪化したのは、政府が何の対策も立てなかったせいだ。
Air pollution got worse because the government took no measures at all.
5. 彼女は何でも人のせいにするから嫌われている。
She is disliked because she blames others for everything.
6. 気のせいか、最近父は元気がないようだ。
Maybe it's just my imagination, but my father seems to be in low spirits lately.
7. 年のせいか、このごろ物忘れがひどい。
Maybe it's because of my age, but lately I've been very forgetful.
8. このあたりは気候が温暖なせいか、のんびりしていて暮らしやすい。
Perhaps thanks to the mild climate, this area is relaxed and easy to live in.
meaning_vi: Because, due to
It seems it's because
explain: Used when you want to mention a reason connected to a bad result
Implies reproach
examples: 1. バスが遅れたせいで、約束の時間に間に合わなかった。
Because the bus was late, I didn't make it in time for the appointment
2. 疲れたせいか、頭が痛い。
Maybe because I'm tired, I have a headache
「～の影響で…といういい結果になる（おかげだ）/よくない結果になる（せいだ）。」 …には希望・意向・相手への働きかけなどの文は来ない。
As an effect of ~, it leads to a good result (thanks to) / it leads to a bad result (because of)
… does not take sentences expressing desire, intention, or urging the listener to do something.
1. いい会社に就職が決まったのは先生のおかげです。ありがとうございました。
It's thanks to you, teacher, that I got a job at a good company. Thank you very much.
2. 天気のいい日が続いたおかげで、工事が早く終わった。
Thanks to a stretch of good weather, the construction finished early.
3. 最近忙しかったせいで、かなり疲れている。
Because I've been busy lately, I'm quite tired.
mistakes: Forgetting の: ×雨せいで → ✓雨のせいで.
Using it with a good result: ×先生のせいで合格した → ✓先生のおかげで合格した.
Choosing the tense of the cause verb: when the cause has already happened, prefer Vたせいで.
Confusing it with ～ために: the JLPT often tests the difference in nuance between "blaming" (せいで) and "neutral" (ために).
Following せいで with a command/request sounds unnatural: use a clause describing an actual result.

<ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>のおかげで<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>した。

fields.meaning: I hear that..., it is said that... (passing on information heard or read)
examples: I hear this department store is focusing on products for young people.
I hear Sakura keeps lots of little flowers in her room.
That cake looks delicious.
He looks well today.
It looks like it's going to rain any minute.
That shop doesn't seem expensive.
fields.explain:
Direct observation → use 様態: images, sounds, signs right in front of you.
Indirect information → use 伝聞: it is good to state the source (～によると/～では); polite: そうです。
Negative of 様態: V なさそうだ / Aい くなさそうだ / Aな ではなさそうだ .
Combinations: そうに + V:嬉しそうに話す (talk happily). そうな + N:面白そうな本(a book that looks interesting).
そうに + V:嬉しそうに話す (talk happily).
そうな + N:面白そうな本(a book that looks interesting).
Avoid using 様態のそうだ with completed past events or facts that are already clearly known.

• 様態のそうだ: Conjecture based on the senses/signs in front of you. Fits signs that 目で見える・耳で聞こえる. Example: 雨が降りそうだ (dark clouds, strong wind...)
• 伝聞のそうだ: Reports information you have heard. Neutral, does not guarantee reliability. Often used with a source: 新聞によると、〜そうだ。
• Do not use 様態のそうだ for inherent qualities that are hard to observe directly (× 日本は安全そうだ in a general sense; use ようだ/らしい instead).
• Contrast of forms: そうだ(様態) means "looks like it's about to / looks", unlike らしい (rumor/characteristic) and ようだ/みたいだ (metaphor/overall comparison).
fields.notes:
• Many nouns describing qualities are actually Aな (元気・幸せ・暇…), so they attach directly to そうだ: 幸せそうだ。
• Colloquial: 死にそう (dead tired), やばそう (looks bad) are used in spoken language.
• 「Aくなさそう」 is more natural than 「Aそうではない」 with Aい.
• 「今にも〜そうだ」 is a frame that emphasizes that something is "about to happen".
meaning_vi: information from letters, magazines, TV, or other people.
examples: 1. ①　弱かったそうだ
I hear (she) was weak.
2. ②　母から聞いたが、姉は子供の時体が弱かったそうだ。
I heard from my mother that my older sister was physically weak as a child.
3. ③　医者に聞いた話では、インフルインザがもう流行しているそうだ。
According to what I heard from the doctor, the flu is already going around.
──────
1. リンさんは子どものころ、サッカーの選手になりたかったそうです。
I hear that as a child, Lin wanted to become a soccer player.
2. 「駅前の新しいレストランに、もう行きましたか」
「Have you been to the new restaurant in front of the station yet?」
3. 「いいえ。でも、チンさんが先週行ったそうです。とてもおいしくて、値段も高くなかったそうです」
「No. But I hear Chin went last week. I hear it was really delicious and not expensive either.」
4. 弟からメールが来た。アリさんはとても歌が上手だそうです。
My younger brother sent an email saying that Ali sings very well.
5. 天気予報によると、明日は一日雨だそうだ。
According to the weather forecast, it will rain all day tomorrow.
6. この本によると、日本では１９５３年にテレビ放送が始まったそうだ。
According to this book, TV broadcasting started in Japan in 1953.
Seems..., I hear...
mistakes: Wrong sound change: × いいそうだ → ○ よさそうだ.
Wrong negative: × 降らないそうだ (if 様態) → ○ 降らなさそうだ. Note: 降らないそうだ is 伝聞.
Using 様態 for general information: × 日本は安全そうだ (use ようだ/らしい).
Confusing そうです (polite) with そうだ (plain): the grammar is the same; only the politeness level differs.

examples: The factory shut down. As a result, the delivery was delayed.
I want to stay healthy. For that purpose, I go jogging every morning.
The budget is insufficient. Therefore, the plan needs to be reviewed.
We want the new product to succeed. To that end, we did thorough market research.
There was heavy snow. Because of that, the school was closed.
fields.explain:
A sentence connective more formal than だから／それで; well suited to essays and reports.
When used with the meaning of "purpose", "そのために" comes before the subsequent actions taken to achieve the stated goal.
Avoid repeating "～ため／ので" in both clauses, which sounds heavy: ×雨のため、そのために中止→ ✓雨で、そのため中止。
A comma after "そのため(に)、" makes the flow of the sentence clearer.

• "そのために" has two interpretations:

Result conjunction: "therefore/for that reason".
Purpose: "in order to do that/to achieve that goal".

• Result conjunction: "therefore/for that reason".
• Purpose: "in order to do that/to achieve that goal".
• When it expresses "result", the first clause states the cause/situation; the second clause states the logical consequence.
• When it expresses "purpose", the first clause states the goal; the second clause is the concrete action taken to achieve that goal.
• In written language, "そのため" (without に) is slightly more formal for the meaning "therefore".
fields.notes:
• When "そのために" expresses purpose, it usually refers back semantically to the goal in the previous sentence; make sure the reference is clear to avoid ambiguity.
• In standard style, "そのため、～" may be preferred for the meaning "therefore".
• Placed at the start of a paragraph to shift the topic: state the cause/vision → そのため、方針…
explain: Used as a connective that continues from a previously stated reason or goal and leads on to the result
examples: 1. 隣の駅で事故があったらしい。そのために電車が遅れている。
Apparently there was an accident at the next station. Because of that, the trains are running late.
2. 留学するつもりだ。そのために、バイトしてお金をためている。
I plan to study abroad. For that, I'm working part-time and saving money
mistakes: Mixing up the meanings "therefore" and "in order to do that" makes the text ambiguous; the JLPT often tests the context to choose the correct one.
Repeating the cause: ×雨のため、そのために～ → omit one of the cause clauses.
Using "そのために" (purpose) when the previous sentence does not clearly state a goal → causes misunderstanding.
Confusing it with それで/だから in formal written language; prefer そのため/その結果/したがって.

<ruby>故障<rt>こしょう</rt></ruby>。そのため<ruby>停止<rt>ていし</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>。それで<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>？

examples: Freshly baked bread smells wonderful.
Please have some freshly brewed coffee.
I'll bring them out freshly fried.
It's freshly made, so it's hot.
I've only just started working, so I still don't know my way around at all.
When I had just joined the company, I was nervous every day.
fields.explain:
Often used for food and "fresh" products: 焼きたて／揚げたて／炊きたて／茹でたて／搾りたて。
Used for a newly reached state: できたて／なりたて／入社したて／結婚したて。
Positive nuance: tasty, fresh, brand-new; sometimes a warning that something is "still hot".
Rarely used with verbs that do not produce a "tangible result" (×食べたて → use 食べたばかり).

• Expresses the state of "having just been done" while the result still keeps its "freshness/newness".
• It is not simply "just happened" in terms of time like 〜たばかり; 〜たて emphasizes the quality of "freshness".
• Lexical restrictions: usually used with verbs that produce a tangible product/result or a new state.
fields.notes:
• Common fixed combinations: 焼きたて・揚げたて・炊きたて・茹でたて・搾りたて・採れたて／とれたて・できたて・入れたて・なりたて・入社したて・結婚したて。
• Negative/affirmative is expressed with だ/です rather than directly on たて: できたてではない（not freshly made）。
• "覚えたて／習いたて" can be used to emphasize the state of "having just learned (still inexperienced)". explain: Used when an action has just finished
Often used with the meaning "fresh, new, piping hot..." ⏐ examples: 1. 焼きたてのパンはおいしい。
Freshly baked bread is delicious
2. あのスーパーは、とりたての新鮮な野菜を売っている。
That supermarket sells fresh, just-picked vegetables
mistakes: Using たて with an unsuitable verb: × 食べたて → √ 食べたばかり。
Taking たて to mean "recently": たて is not used for something that "just happened" in general (× 昨日起きたて). Use 起きたばかり.
Wrong form with する-verbs: × 勉強したて? → 勉強したて is possible, but 勉強し始めたばかり is more natural depending on the context.
Attaching it directly to an adjective: × 新しいたて → use できたて／作りたて to express "newly made".

rows: できたて vs できたばかり
できたて: emphasizes being "brand-new"; できたばかり: emphasizes time
できたてのケーキ／できたばかりのケーキ

fields.meaning: Used to give an example of the words or sentence that come before.
examples: I'd like to try a Japanese sport, for example, judo.
Yamada always gets home late. For example, yesterday he got home at 11.
For example, cake, chocolate, and so on.
In an emergency, for example, in case of an accident or illness.
I often listen to music. For example, classical, jazz, and so on.
fields.notes: Used when showing something mentioned before by giving a concrete example. When a hypothetical case is given as an example, as in ⑤ and ⑥, it is followed by 「とすると」, 「としたら」, etc.

examples: Even if it's a little expensive, I want to buy something of good quality.
Even if my parents are against it, I want to leave home and live on my own.
Even if your handwriting is poor, a handwritten letter feels warmer.
Even a small child should understand if you speak slowly to them.
Even if it rains, the game will be held.
Even if I fail, I will keep trying.
fields.explain:
Often used in statements of determination/policy: たとえ〜ても、〜する。
The second clause is rarely a direct request to the listener unless it has a soft nuance: たとえ〜でも、〜してください。
In spoken language, たとえ can be omitted, using only 〜ても/〜でも; adding たとえ adds emphasis.
Combines well with emphatic words: いくら／どんなに／たとえ…

• Expresses hypothetical concession: "Even if ... (still) ...".
• たとえ is an emphatic adverb; grammatically it can be omitted, but it is added to strengthen the emphasis.
• The second clause is usually a volition/determination/evaluation unaffected by the preceding condition.
• Used for hypothetical or possible situations; not used to describe obvious facts.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ても (ordinary concession).
→ たとえ～ても gives strong emphasis: "no matter what, still...".
2) The second clause is usually a firm conclusion.
→ Often volition/decision/assertion (will still do it, will not change).
3) Not suitable when only stating a slight possibility.
→ For an ordinary "even if... still...", ～ても is enough. meaning_vi: Supposing that... even so... / Even if... still... ⏐ explain: Used when you want to emphasize the assertion of a fact or action regardless of other conditions occurring ⏐ examples: 1. たとえ反対されても留学します。
Even if people are against it, I will study abroad
2. たとえ元気じゃなくても、家族への手紙には元気だと書きます。
Even if I'm not well, I write in letters to my family that I'm fine
mistakes: Wrong particle with N/なA: × たとえ雨ても → √ たとえ雨でも。
Omitting たとえ when the question requires emphasis; on the JLPT, it can be a trap choice between "ても" and "たとえ〜ても".
Using it for obvious facts → unnatural: × たとえ火は熱くても（everyone knows this, so no concession is needed).
A blunt command/prohibition in the second clause: × たとえ遅れても来るな → use a softer expression or change the structure.

fields.meaning:
たとえ～しても→（-）の予想(よそう)・判断(はんだん)、たいしたことではない
Even if
examples: Even if I told the truth, nobody would believe me.
With this illness, recovery is thought to be difficult even with surgery.
"Even if you hurry now, you won't make it."
What's done is done; regretting it now won't change anything.
She has a lot of stamina, so she'd probably be fine even after staying up two or three nights.
Just as I finished writing the last answer, the exam ended.
fields.explain: ◎ The preceding event has just finished when the following event occurs.

examples: The moment I got out of the car, I smelled the sea.
The moment I saw my teacher's face, I realized I had forgotten to do my homework.
The moment I opened the door, the cat dashed out.
The moment I sat down, the phone started ringing.
The moment I saw his face, tears welled up.
The moment I left the house, it started raining hard.
fields.explain:
Has the nuance of narrating a sudden event, quick as "the blink of an eye".
The second clause is not used to express the speaker's intention (commands, advice, invitations...).
Often accompanied by emphatic 副詞: そのとたん(に), ちょうどそのとたん(に).
Often used with verbs of sudden change: 降り出す, 鳴る, 壊れる, 飛び出す, 立ち上がる, こみ上げる.
Has a narrative nuance; suitable for written language and moderately formal speech.

• Expresses something that happens instantly, right after the action in the first clause is finished.
• The second clause is usually an unexpected result, beyond one's intention/control, and very sudden.
• Usually used in the past to narrate events that have happened; rarely used for predicted future events.
• The subjects of the two clauses can differ, but the second clause should not express volition, a command, or an invitation.
• Unlike ～たら/～とすぐ: ～とたん emphasizes suddenness and unexpectedness at that very moment.
fields.notes:
• "とたん" can be written in kana: とたんに. The form "そのとたん" refers to exactly the moment just mentioned.
• Negating an unexpected emotion is rare: the second clause is usually an objective occurrence.
• In narratives, "とたん" speeds up the rhythm and creates an unexpected climax.
• Similar structures: "～や/～や否や" is limited to written language; "～か～ないかのうちに" emphasizes an extremely short interval.
mistakes: Using volition/a command in the second clause: × ドアを開けたとたん、入ろう。→ Use instead: 開けたら入ろう。
Using it for a prolonged action: × 仕事を始めたとたん、三時間働いた。→ Not suitable because it is not sudden.
Using the present tense/a future prediction: × 行くとたん、雨が降るだろう。→ Narrating the past is natural.
Confusing it with ～たらすぐ: ～とたん requires unexpectedness; ～たらすぐ is neutral and allows commands.
The subject being the speaker but expressing a sudden sensation is fine: 立ち上がったとたん、めまいがした (not a trap).
